Rueppell's vulture, Gyps rueppellii, exhibits a series of well-defined life-history milestones that are closely tied to thermal conditions, particularly during the critical early developmental period. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after an incubation period of approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days], a duration that is relatively extended compared to many other accipitrid raptors and likely reflects the substantial yolk reserves required to support the developing embryo. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are surprisingly small given the species' eventual large size, with newly hatched chicks weighing roughly 100 grams [Wwb = roughly 100 grams]. This relatively modest neonatal mass places them at a distinct energetic disadvantage, necessitating an intense period of biparental provisioning to fuel rapid somatic growth. The thermal environment during incubation is thus a critical determinant of hatching success and the subsequent condition of the newly emerged nestling.

Growth proceeds at a remarkable pace within the nest, with the altricial chick undergoing a rapid transformation from a downy, dependent neonate into a fully feathered juvenile capable of flight. The nestling achieves the capacity for sustained flight and fledges from the nest at approximately 150 days after hatching [tx = approximately 150 days after hatching], a milestone attained under the warm 40 °C [T = 40 °C] conditions typical of its Sub-Saharan breeding grounds. This extended nestling period is among the longest documented for any vulture species and is believed to be a consequence of the high energetic demands of attaining a very large adult body size. The achievement of fledging marks a critical juncture, as the young bird must then transition from complete dependence on parental regurgitation to acquiring carrion independently, a skill that requires considerable learning and physical prowess.

Following fledging, the immature bird enters a protracted juvenile phase characterized by continued skeletal growth and the attainment of full adult mass. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown adult Rueppell's vulture is approximately 8,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 8,500 grams], a figure that places it among the heaviest of the Old World vultures. Field records indicate that this adult body mass can range from roughly 6,400 to 9,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 6,400 to 9,000 grams], depending on individual condition and seasonal food availability. The physiological maturation process is slow, and the onset of gonadal activity is not triggered until the bird has reached a substantial fraction of its ultimate size. Under the consistent thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] that characterize the active season, puberty is attained at approximately 450 days after hatching [tp = approximately 450 days after hatching], representing a significant post-fledging developmental delay.

The transition to full reproductive status is marked by a further deferral of breeding activity. Although individuals become physiologically capable of reproduction at puberty, first successful breeding events are typically postponed for several more years as the young birds establish territories and acquire the foraging experience necessary to provision a chick. The time since birth at first brood for Rueppell's vulture is documented at roughly 1,460 days [tR = roughly 1,460 days], again under ambient conditions near 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delayed onset of reproduction is a common life-history strategy among long-lived, large-bodied avian species, where the benefits of investing in clutch production must be carefully weighed against the survival prospects of both the parent and the offspring. The extended pre-breeding period allows for the complete refinement of soaring and scavenging skills.

Rueppell's vulture is characterized by a remarkably slow life-history pace, consistent with its position as a top scavenger in a resource-poor environment. The maximum reproductive output of a breeding pair is constrained by the long rearing period and the delayed age at first breeding. A female can successfully fledge, on average, only one chick per year [Ri = one chick per year], representing the maximum possible reproductive rate for the species. The lifespan for this species is a subject of ongoing research; while comparative records from closely related species with similar body plans provide context, definitive data for Gyps rueppellii are still emerging. In the interim, the maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 41.4 years [am = approximately 41.4 years], a value borrowed from the closely related Eurasian griffon vulture (Gyps fulvus) at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].
